facts.text: The funeral eulogy invokes the Wizard of Oz's Tin Man. The film's only listed movie reference on IMDb is The Wizard of Oz (1939).
Killer Party went through the working titles Fool's Night and April Fool. It became Killer Party when Paramount announced its own April Fool's Day, due in theaters first.
Director William Fruet co-wrote the classic Canadian road movie Goin' Down the Road. His own debut, Wedding in White (1972), won Best Picture at the 1973 Canadian Film Awards.
Critic Tim Brayton noted the opening stacks a funeral inside a drive-in movie inside a music video. The film's title doesn't appear until about nine and a quarter minutes in.
Goof alert: as April wanders the abandoned snack bar, the film crew can be seen reflected in the silver metal of the candy case.
The song over the opening is 'You're No Fool', performed by the band White Sister. It is credited to the character April in the film's music listing.
Elaine Wilkes (Phoebe) left acting and earned a Ph.D. in naturopathy, plus a master's in psychology. She later became a LEED-accredited green building professional.
The fictional Briggs College, where the sorority sisters study, turns up again in the 1998 slasher Urban Legend.
After shooting in 1984, MGM reportedly left the film on the shelf for a year and a half, per The Tampa Tribune's Bob Ross. It then got only a limited US release.
The ad tagline read 'DEADicated to the class of '86.' Another promised: 'By the end of the dance, some of the sorority sisters were dead on their feet.'
Goof alert: when the killer approaches the housemother nailing down a stair, the camera's shadow is visible on the door to the right.
Filming began in Toronto in fall 1984, but the film didn't reach theaters until May 9, 1986. It was a US/Canada co-production.
Professor Zito is named after director Joseph Zito, who made Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter (1984). Killer Party screenwriter Barney Cohen wrote that film too.
Paul Bartel (Professor Zito) directed Death Race 2000 and the cult hit Eating Raoul. He appeared in over 90 films and TV episodes, often opposite Mary Woronov.
Ralph Seymour (Martin) began on Broadway in Peter Shaffer's Equus. He later appeared in Empire of the Sun (1987) and Rain Man (1988).
Martin Hewitt (Blake) was a bartender and valet parker before he beat out 5,000 actors, reportedly including Tom Cruise and Timothy Hutton, to star in Endless Love (1981).
Richard Scheib of Moria gave it two stars. He praised Sherry Willis-Burch's lively performance but noted nearly an hour passes before the killings start.
John Beal's score mixes live strings and brass with synths including a Fairlight CMI and a Yamaha DX7. He also slipped in a Bernard Herrmann-style riff, per a Blu-ray.com review.
When Sherry Willis-Burch auditioned, Vivia was a small role and the first character to die. After she won it, the script was rewritten and the part was expanded.
Elaine Wilkes (Phoebe) said the film was significantly altered after shooting. In editing, one character's real death was replaced with a fake-out joke.
Joanna Johnson (Jennifer) went on to a long soap career, playing on and off on The Bold and the Beautiful from 1987 to 2014.
Sherry Willis-Burch (Vivia) also starred in an earlier slasher, Final Exam (1981), where she played Janet.
Writer Barney Cohen's Killer Party reunited the horror-comedy prank with the slasher. Film Society of Lincoln Center called it an overlooked slasher, overshadowed by April Fool's Day.
Screenwriter Barney Cohen says the film's working title was The April Fool. A copyright dispute arose with the financiers of Friday the 13th Part IV, who were making April Fool's Day.
The grocery bags in this scene are from Bells Supermarket, a Western New York chain that went out of business seven years after the film came out.
Filmed in October, though this half is set on April 1. You can spot actors in winter coats and even snowflakes drifting past the camera in exterior shots.
The slow-dance song, 'The Lucky One', was performed by Laura Branigan and written by Bruce Roberts.
Two of the actresses wore contact lenses on set. Gas-permeable lenses were standard in 1984 and bulkier than today's, which made them awkward to work in.
MGM cut bloody details from almost every murder before release. Fangoria magazine then published photos of the trimmed death scenes. They were never restored.
The pre-cut version had more gore, including a fuller trident impalement of sorority sister Pam. The MPAA demanded cuts and the film was re-edited.
It was the last film in MGM's original library, dating to 1924, released the same month Kirk Kerkorian sold the studio to Ted Turner. It grossed just $457,026.
Critic Tim Brayton counted twelve deaths in the film and called it several different movies in one: teen comedy, sex farce, mystery and slasher.
Goof alert: forearm splints are visible under Jennifer's sleeves when she blocks blows from wooden beams. Her sleeves roll up once, then back down to hide them.
Joe Bob Briggs gave the film a slight recommendation for its sheer number of murders. He felt its supernatural elements recalled The Exorcist and Poltergeist.
Director William Fruet moved into TV, including Goosebumps and Poltergeist: The Legacy. LA's New Beverly Cinema ran a triple-feature retrospective of his work in 2015.
Per TCM, the final ambulance scene was shot around 3 a.m. The distributor also toned down the film's gore, especially in the finale, to get an R rating.
